title: Syllogisms

blocks.title: What 'follows' means
blocks.markdown:
A syllogism gives two or more statements built from **All**, **Some** and **No**, then a few conclusions. You must say which conclusions **follow**.

A conclusion follows only if it is true in **every** arrangement the statements allow. If you can draw even one valid picture where the conclusion fails, it does not follow. Treat the statements as certainly true, however odd they sound, and never bring in outside knowledge about the real things named.

blocks.title: Draw the statements as circles
blocks.markdown:
Each statement is a picture:

- **All A are B:** circle A drawn entirely inside circle B.
- **No A is B:** circle A and circle B drawn apart, not touching.
- **Some A are B:** circle A and circle B drawn overlapping, with at least one item in the shared part.

Draw the first statement, then add the second so that both stay true at once, then read the conclusions off the combined picture. Where the second statement could be added in more than one way, you must try each way.

blocks.title: How 'Some' and 'All' behave
blocks.markdown:
- **Some A are B does not rule out All A are B.** "Some" here means "at least one", not "only some". So a valid picture for "Some A are B" may have A completely inside B.
- **Some A are B also gives Some B are A.** Overlap works both ways.
- **All A are B gives Some B are A** (taking the classes to be non-empty), but it does **not** give All B are A.
- **No A is B gives No B is A.**

These conversions are the conclusions that most often follow directly from a single statement.

blocks.title: Testing a conclusion
blocks.markdown:
For each conclusion, ask: **can I draw the statements, all true, so that this conclusion is false?**

- If **yes**, you have a counter-picture, and the conclusion does **not** follow.
- If **no** — every valid picture keeps it true — the conclusion **follows**.

Be systematic. List the ways the statements can combine (usually two or three), draw each, and check the conclusion against all of them. A conclusion that holds in two pictures but fails in the third does not follow.

blocks.title: Possibility and either-or conclusions
blocks.markdown:
**Possibility conclusions** are worded "Some A being C is a possibility" or "All A being B is a possibility". Such a conclusion follows if **at least one** valid picture shows it. It fails only when **no** valid picture can show it — for instance, when a part of A is already forced to lie outside C.

**Either-or conclusions** come in a pair. When neither conclusion of the pair follows on its own, but together they cover **every** valid picture — usually because they are exact opposites, such as "Some A are B" and "No A is B" — the answer is "either the first or the second follows".

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.markdown:
**Set 1.** Statements: All pens are books. All books are files. Conclusions: (I) All pens are files. (II) Some files are pens.

Pens sit inside books, and books sit inside files, so pens sit inside files. (I) follows. Pens exist and are files, so some files are pens; (II) follows. **Both follow.**

**Set 2.** Statements: Some cups are plates. No plate is a spoon. Conclusions: (I) Some cups are not spoons. (II) Some cups being spoons is a possibility.

The cups that are plates cannot be spoons, and that group is non-empty, so (I) follows. The cups outside the plate overlap are free to be spoons, so (II) — a possibility — also follows. **Both follow.**

**Set 3.** Statements: All roads are paths. Some paths are lanes. Conclusions: (I) Some roads are lanes. (II) No road is a lane.

The lane overlap on paths may or may not reach into the roads. If it does, (I) is true and (II) is false; if it does not, some picture has the roads clear of lanes, making (II) true and (I) false. Exactly one of them holds in every picture, so the answer is **either (I) or (II) follows**.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.markdown:
- **Reading "Some" as "only some"**, and rejecting a picture where A lies wholly inside B.
- **Converting "All A are B" to "All B are A".** Only "Some B are A" follows.
- **Checking one picture.** A conclusion must survive every valid combination.
- **Linking two end terms** through nothing — from "All A are B" and "Some C are D" nothing about A and C follows.
- **Calling a possibility false** without checking that *no* picture can show it.
- **Missing an either-or pair** by testing the two conclusions only one at a time.

blocks.title: Quick revision
blocks.markdown:
- A conclusion follows only if it is true in every valid picture; one counter-picture kills it.
- Draw All as one circle inside another, No as separate circles, Some as an overlap.
- "Some" means at least one and allows "All"; "Some A are B" gives "Some B are A"; "All A are B" gives only "Some B are A"; "No A is B" gives "No B is A".
- A possibility follows if one valid picture shows it, and fails only if none can.
- If neither of two conclusions follows alone but together they cover every picture — usually exact opposites — the answer is either-or.

blocks.title: Practice
blocks.markdown:
For each set say which follows: I only, II only, both, neither, or either-or. Give a one-line reason.

1. All cats are dogs. All dogs are animals. (I) All cats are animals. (II) Some animals are cats.
2. No book is a pen. All pens are pencils. (I) Some pencils are not books. (II) No book is a pencil.
3. Some apples are red. Some red things are sweet. (I) Some apples are sweet. (II) No apple is sweet.
4. All keys are locks. No lock is a door. (I) No key is a door. (II) Some keys are locks.
5. Some pens are inks. All inks are blue. (I) Some pens are blue. (II) All pens being blue is a possibility.
6. All trees are plants. Some plants are green. (I) Some trees are green. (II) Some trees are not green.
7. No fan is a cooler. Some coolers are air conditioners. (I) Some air conditioners are not fans. (II) All air conditioners being fans is a possibility.

flashcards.back: Only when it is true in every arrangement the statements allow. A single valid picture where it fails means it does not follow.
flashcards.explanation: Take the statements as true and use no outside knowledge.

flashcards.front: How do you draw All A are B, No A is B, and Some A are B?
flashcards.back: All A are B: circle A inside circle B. No A is B: the two circles apart. Some A are B: the two circles overlapping with something in the shared part.
flashcards.explanation: Every statement is one of these three pictures.

flashcards.front: Does 'Some A are B' rule out 'All A are B'?
flashcards.back: No. 'Some' means 'at least one', so a valid picture for 'Some A are B' may have A entirely inside B.
flashcards.explanation: Reading 'some' as 'only some' is the classic error.

flashcards.front: From 'All A are B', what converse follows?
flashcards.back: 'Some B are A' (the classes being non-empty). 'All B are A' does not follow.
flashcards.explanation: 'No A is B' converts fully: 'No B is A'.

flashcards.front: How do you test whether a conclusion follows?
flashcards.back: Try to draw the statements, all true, so that the conclusion is false. If you can, it does not follow; if every valid picture keeps it true, it follows.
flashcards.explanation: Be systematic: list the ways the statements can combine and check all of them.

flashcards.front: When does a possibility conclusion follow?
flashcards.back: When at least one valid picture shows it. It fails only if no valid picture can show it.
flashcards.explanation: A part of A already forced outside C is what makes 'Some A being C is a possibility' fail.

flashcards.front: When is the answer 'either I or II follows'?
flashcards.back: When neither conclusion follows on its own, but together they cover every valid picture — typically because they are exact opposites like 'Some A are B' and 'No A is B'.
flashcards.explanation: Test the pair together, not just one at a time.
